case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Magazu v. Department of Children and Families
key_cases.holding: The SJC upheld the department's denial of a foster and preadoptive parent application based on the applicants' religiously motivated use of corporal punishment on their own children, holding the decision was supported by substantial evidence and that the substantial burden on the applicants' religious exercise was outweighed by the Commonwealth's compelling interest in protecting foster children.
key_cases.relevance: Magazu is the leading Massachusetts decision rejecting a religious-discrimination challenge to a foster placement licensing denial, and it supplies the framework any such claim must meet.
key_cases.quote: Consistent with this compelling State interest, the department has determined that a foster child should not be placed in a home where corporal punishment is used as a disciplinary measure.

key_cases.holding: The Appeals Court affirmed termination, holding that homelessness, poverty and financial instability cannot alone support termination but may properly be considered as part of the unfitness determination where they are tied to the parent's inability to provide minimally adequate care.
key_cases.relevance: Virgil is the closest Massachusetts appellate guard against terminating parental rights on grounds that are effectively economic status.
key_cases.quote: While homelessness, poverty, and financial instability alone are not sufficient to terminate a person's parental rights, they are proper considerations in an unfitness determination.

key_cases.holding: The SJC held that the Juvenile Court properly exercised jurisdiction to adjudicate a child in need of care and protection and to dispense with the consent of a father who was a foreign national in the United States on a temporary work visa, and affirmed the finding of unfitness as overwhelmingly supported.
key_cases.relevance: Peggy rejects the contention that a parent's foreign nationality limits the court's authority, while requiring the same clear and convincing proof of unfitness as in any other case.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the Juvenile Court properly exercised jurisdiction and now affirm the decree.

key_cases.holding: The SJC affirmed the judgment dispensing with the parents' consent to adoption, holding that a proceeding to terminate parental rights is not a "service, program, or activity" so the Americans with Disabilities Act may not be raised as a defense to it, while holding that the ADA, Massachusetts antidiscrimination law and the State Constitution do require the department to accommodate a disabled parent's special needs in the services it provides beforehand, and that the department did so here.
key_cases.relevance: Gregory is the leading Massachusetts authority on disability discrimination in child welfare: the ADA is no defense to termination, but the department must accommodate a disabled parent in the services it renders.
key_cases.quote: the ADA, as well as Massachusetts anti-discrimination laws, regulations, and our Constitution all require the department to accommodate the parents' special needs in its provision of services

key_cases.holding: The SJC reversed a Probate and Family Court judgment denying a mother's petition to remove the guardian and regain custody of her two children, holding that the findings were inadequate because unfitness must be predicated on parental behavior that adversely affects the child and there was no evidence in the record connecting the mother's lesbian household to her fitness as a parent.
key_cases.relevance: Bezio is the foundational Massachusetts holding that a parent's lifestyle or status cannot support a custody deprivation absent a demonstrated nexus to harm to the child.
key_cases.quote: A finding that a parent is unfit to further the welfare of the child must be predicated upon parental behavior which adversely affects the child.
